summary: Children aged 7–9 learn the procedure of measuring and recording weather: reading a thermometer (°C), a rain gauge (mm), a wind vane (direction) and an anemometer (speed), keeping a weather diary over at least a week, and turning the recorded table into a bar graph/pictograph so a pattern emerges. The core objective is a hands-on measure-and-record skill performed over time, with accurate scale-reading and consistent (same place, same time) measurement, culminating in the move from raw readings to a data representation.
misconceptions: A wind vane measures wind SPEED — it shows DIRECTION; the anemometer measures speed
The rain gauge shows total rain ever — it is read then emptied for each period
Reading a thermometer from an angle gives the true value — must read at eye level
Any single reading describes the weather — patterns need repeated, consistent measurements over time
Bigger numbers are always 'more weather' — units and what is measured matter (mm of rain vs °C)

activities.title: Weather-station logbook: read, record, graph
steps: Each 'day', read the thermometer to the nearest °C with your eye level with the top of the liquid, read the rain gauge in mm on a flat surface at the meniscus, note the direction the wind vane arrow points, and read the anemometer for wind speed (for example in km/h, or as spins counted in a set time on a homemade anemometer).
Write each reading into a weather-diary table with its date and unit (e.g. 12°C, 4 mm, wind from the west, wind speed 10 km/h or 15 spins in 30 seconds).
Repeat the routine for at least a week, keeping the place and time of day the same each day.
After a week, turn the table into a bar graph or pictograph with equal, labelled axis intervals, then read the pattern aloud (e.g. 'a run of cold wet days, then a warm dry spell').
Say why scientists measure consistently over time rather than relying on a single reading.
activities.insight: A single reading is real data, but it only shows one moment; a week of consistent, correctly-unit-ed readings becomes a data story, and a graph makes the pattern leap out of numbers that looked scattered — the step from measurement to representation.

activities.title: Match each instrument to its quantity and unit
steps: Pair each instrument with the quantity it measures and the unit used: thermometer → temperature → °C; rain gauge → rainfall → mm; wind vane → wind direction; anemometer → wind speed.
Explain in your own words why a wind vane does NOT measure speed and why the anemometer does.
Given a number with a unit (e.g. 15 mm, 15°C), say what was measured and why the unit matters — a bigger number is not simply 'more weather'.
activities.insight: Each instrument measures a specific quantity in a specific unit; knowing the pairing is the foundation for choosing the right tool and reading it correctly.

activities.title: Check the skill: read a scale and interpret a graph
steps: Read a shown thermometer to the nearest °C, placing your eye level with the top of the liquid.

Given a completed weekly bar graph, answer questions about the pattern (e.g. which day was warmest, whether the week was mostly wet or dry, what the weather was usually like that week, and why more weeks of data would be needed to describe a whole season).
Spot and fix a problem reading: a tilted rain gauge, a wind direction reported backwards, or a graph with unlabelled axes.
activities.insight: A correct reading plus a correct interpretation of the graph shows the procedure has been learned, not just recognised.

checkQuestion: Set out a thermometer, a rain gauge and a wind vane (homemade versions are fine). Ask the child to take today's reading from each, record it on a simple chart with the date, and after several days turn the readings into a bar or line graph. Watch how they place and read each instrument and build the graph — don't ask them to explain the instruments, watch them use them.
checkAnswer: Reads the thermometer at eye level to the correct scale in °C, reads the rain gauge on a level surface at the meniscus, reads wind direction from the vane correctly (the arrow points to where the wind comes FROM), records each with date and units, and transfers the log into a correctly-scaled, labelled graph.
